items.title: Dorothy Donegan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Jo Jones was sort of a mentor. He was psychic, that’s what Jimmy says. He liked to talk rough to you. ... He threw a stick at me, you got that?

ctx.x: Oh, did Jo know her too?

items.title: Dorothy Donegan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And so, we’d be on the road. I discovered you don’t go with people you work with.

ctx.x: When was this? J.C. Heard? Tell me about him.

They called him “Swee-dee-dee.” And he was sort of on the pimpy side. But that didn’t hurt me, you know. But he was a good drummer. So, we’d be on the road. I discovered you don’t go with people you work with. You can’t ‘S’ where you eat. And so pretty soon, that broke up.
How long did it take before you learned that?

items.title: 68642_Jo Jones oral history interview
items.q: I did a little house there with Dorothy Donegan and Joe Bushkin and Tyree Glenn.

ctx.x: Eddie Locke - he's a great drummer -

He's playing with Roy Budd Johnson thing. I used to sit down and tell them, "You're going to play with Earl Hines. You're going to play with Teddy Wilson. You're going to play with Dorothy Donegan. You're going to play with this. You're going to Newport. You're going to Europe." "I am?" I'd say, "Sure you are." "When?" I'd say, "You'll find out." So they found out. I had to tell them now, you see. You know how difficult it is to have a group that's going to stay together for 4 or 5 years, with economic situation…
Let's take a little break... and wet our throats a little here.
